## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Chapter 11: Hypothesis testing with randomization](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/foundations-randomization.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You will learn to frame a research question as a null and an alternative hypothesis, to build a null distribution by shuffling the results of an experiment, and to measure the evidence against the null hypothesis with a p-value, using experiments on sex discrimination in promotions and on how students spend money.

### Exercise 1

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `hypothesis-testing-with-randomization`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it. You may need to restart this tutorial after you do so.

Create a new file, `analysis.qmd`, with the title `"Hypothesis Testing with Randomization"` and your name as the author. In a bash Terminal, render it:

```bash
quarto render analysis.qmd
```

Open `analysis.html` with Live Server (right-click it in the Explorer → **Open with Live Server**) and keep the tab open. It refreshes on every render. Going forward, we will just tell you to "Render" when we want you to take these steps.

Create a `.gitignore` with `analysis_files` followed by a blank line. Commit and push. Use AI however you like.

If `show_file()` fails, it is probably because you have not yet loaded `library(learnr2)` in the R Terminal.

###

**infer** writes every randomization test as the same four steps: name the variables, state the null hypothesis, generate shuffled datasets, and calculate a statistic from each one. The book's authors used it to draw every simulated distribution in this chapter.

## Sex discrimination case study

"We consider a study investigating sex discrimination in the 1970s, which is set in the context of personnel decisions within a bank." The research question: "Are individuals who identify as female discriminated against in promotion decisions made by their managers who identify as male?"

### Exercise 1

Add a chunk that prints `sex_discrimination`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-1-test
#| echo: true
sex_discrimination
```

###

Each of the 48 rows is one personnel file, judged by one bank supervisor: `sex` is the sex the file listed and `decision` is the supervisor's recommendation. "The files given to the participants were identical, except that half of them indicated the candidate identified as male and the other half indicated the candidate identified as female."

### Exercise 2

```{.output}
Description:

     recommendations.

Format:

     A data frame with 48 observations on the following 2 variables.

     sex a factor with levels ‘female’ and ‘male’

     decision a factor with levels ‘not promoted’ and ‘promoted’

Source:

     Rosen B and Jerdee T. 1974. Influence of sex role stereotypes on
     personnel decisions. Journal of Applied Psychology 59(1):9-14.
```

###

"The participants in this study were 48 bank supervisors who identified as male, attending a management institute at the University of North Carolina in 1972." The study "considered sex roles," allowing only male and female, so its categories are not gender identities.

The help page lists `female` before `male` and `not promoted` before `promoted`, but the data stores them the other way around. Level order matters: a difference in proportions subtracts one level from the other, and the chapter reports male minus female.


###

Supervisors promoted 21 of the 24 male files and 14 of the 24 female files, 35 promotions in all. "These files were randomly assigned to the bank managers," which makes the study an experiment.

### Exercise 5

Replace the code in that chunk so that it calculates the proportion of files promoted for each `sex`. Render.

```{r}

#| echo: false

```

```{r}
  summarize(prop_promoted = mean(decision == "promoted"),
            .by = sex)
```

###

Male files were promoted 87.5% of the time and female files 58.3%. Still, "it is unclear whether the difference provides *convincing evidence* that individuals who identify as female are unfairly discriminated against."

### Exercise 6

Replace the code in that chunk so that it uses **infer** to calculate the difference in the proportion promoted, male minus female, with `promoted` as the outcome of interest. Store the result as `sex_obs` and print it. Render.

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-6-test
#| echo: true
sex_obs <- sex_discrimination |>
  specify(decision ~ sex, success = "promoted") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("male", "female"))

sex_obs
```

###

The gap is 0.292, or 29.2 percentage points, and "this observed difference is what we call a **point estimate** of the true difference." The **null hypothesis** says "the variables `sex` and `decision` are independent," and the **alternative hypothesis** says they are not.

### Exercise 7

If sex made no difference, the 35 promotions could have landed on any 35 files. Below `sex_obs`, replace the line that prints it with code that shuffles the decisions across the 48 files once, as if sex and decision were independent, and counts the shuffled files by `sex` and `decision`. Set a seed of 9 first, so that your shuffle can match ours. Render.

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-7-test
#| echo: true
sex_obs <- sex_discrimination |>
  specify(decision ~ sex, success = "promoted") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("male", "female"))

set.seed(9)
sex_discrimination |>
  specify(decision ~ sex, success = "promoted") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1, type = "permute") |>
  count(sex, decision)
```

###

Our shuffle promoted 17 male files and 18 female files, and the totals are still 35 promoted and 13 not; your counts will differ if your shuffle did. "Since the randomization of files in this simulation is independent of the promotion decisions, any difference in promotion rates is due to chance."

### Exercise 8

Change the shuffle so that, instead of counting, it calculates the difference in the proportion promoted, male minus female, for the shuffled files. Render.

```{r}
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("male", "female"))

set.seed(9)
sex_discrimination |>

  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("male", "female"))
```

###

Our shuffle gives -0.042, the chapter's first shuffle gave 0.042, and the real study gave 0.292. "We call the summary value the **statistic** of interest (or often the **test statistic**)."

### Exercise 9

Change the code so that it shuffles the files 100 times, calculating the difference for each shuffle, and stores the 100 differences as `sex_null`. Set the seed to 37, the one the chapter used, and print `sex_null`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-9-test

  specify(decision ~ sex, success = "promoted") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("male", "female"))

set.seed(37)
sex_null <- sex_discrimination |>
  specify(decision ~ sex, success = "promoted") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 100, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("male", "female"))

sex_null
```

###

Each row is one sham experiment, and the differences bounce around zero: -0.042, 0.042, -0.125, and so on. "Note that the distribution of these simulated differences in proportions is centered around 0."

### Exercise 10

Replace the line that prints `sex_null` with code that counts how many of the 100 shuffled differences are at least as large as `sex_obs`, and what proportion of the 100 that is. Render.

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-10
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-10-test
#| echo: true
sex_obs <- sex_discrimination |>
  specify(decision ~ sex, success = "promoted") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("male", "female"))

set.seed(37)
sex_null <- sex_discrimination |>
  specify(decision ~ sex, success = "promoted") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 100, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("male", "female"))

sex_null |>
  summarize(n_extreme = sum(stat >= sex_obs$stat),
            prop_extreme = mean(stat >= sex_obs$stat))
```

###

Two of our 100 shuffles reached 0.292, exactly as in the chapter's figure, which used the same seed. "Such a low probability indicates that observing such a large difference from chance alone is rare."

### Exercise 11

Change the number of shuffles from 100 to 1,000. Render.

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: sex-discrimination-case-study-11-test
#| echo: true
sex_obs <- sex_discrimination |>
  specify(decision ~ sex, success = "promoted") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("male", "female"))

set.seed(37)
sex_null <- sex_discrimination |>
  specify(decision ~ sex, success = "promoted") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("male", "female"))

sex_null |>
  summarize(n_extreme = sum(stat >= sex_obs$stat),
            prop_extreme = mean(stat >= sex_obs$stat))
```

###

Now 24 of 1,000 shuffles reach 0.292, a proportion of 0.024, close to the chapter's 2 in 100; your count may differ a little. More shuffles give "a good idea of the shape of the *distribution of differences* under the null hypothesis."

Color the bars at or beyond the observed difference differently from the rest, make the vertical line dashed, show the x-axis as percentages, move the legend below the plot, and add a title, axis labels, a subtitle that states the main finding, and a caption giving the number of supervisors, the number of shuffles, and the source.   scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
```{r}
  labs(title = "Promotion Gaps in 1,000 Shuffled Experiments",

       y = "Number of Shuffles",
       fill = NULL,
       caption = "48 bank supervisors; 1,000 random shuffles of the files\nRosen and Jerdee (1974)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

###

"When we conduct formal studies, we reject a null position (the idea that the data are a result of chance only) if the data strongly conflict with that null position." Here, the chapter concludes, "we reject the null hypothesis in favor of the alternative."

## Opportunity cost case study

The chapter explores "whether reminding students about this well-known fact about money causes them to be a little thriftier": that "money not spent now can be spent later." Researchers ran an experiment on 150 students to find out.

### Exercise 1

Start a new chunk that prints `opportunity_cost`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: opportunity-cost-case-study-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: opportunity-cost-case-study-1-test
#| echo: true
opportunity_cost
```

###

Each of the 150 rows is one student "at a university in the southwestern United States," with the `group` the researchers assigned and the `decision` the student made. Every student read the same offer of a video "for a special sale price of \$14.99."

### Exercise 2


###

```{.output}
Format:

     A data frame with 150 observations on the following 2 variables.

     group a factor with levels ‘control’ and ‘treatment’

     decision a factor with levels ‘buy video’ and ‘not buy video’

Source:

     Frederick S, Novemsky N, Wang J, Dhar R, Nowlis S. 2009.
     Opportunity Cost Neglect. Journal of Consumer Research 36:
     553-561.
```

###

The only difference between the groups was one added sentence in option (B): "Keep the \$14.99 for other purchases." The chapter admits that "this context might feel strange if physical video stores predate you."

### Exercise 6

Replace the code in that chunk so that it uses **infer** to calculate the difference in the proportion who chose not to buy, treatment minus control. Store the result as `opp_obs` and print it. Render.

The point estimate is 0.200; without an explicit order, **infer** would subtract in level order, control minus treatment, report -0.200, and warn you. The null hypothesis: "Reminding students that they can save money for later purchases will not have any impact on students' spending decisions."

### Exercise 7

Below `opp_obs`, replace the line that prints it with code that shuffles the decisions across the 150 students 1,000 times, calculates the difference, treatment minus control, for each shuffle, and stores the 1,000 differences as `opp_null`. Set the seed to 25, the one the chapter used, and print `opp_null`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: opportunity-cost-case-study-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: opportunity-cost-case-study-7-test
#| echo: true
opp_obs <- opportunity_cost |>
  specify(decision ~ group, success = "not buy video") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("treatment", "control"))

set.seed(25)
opp_null <- opportunity_cost |>
  specify(decision ~ group, success = "not buy video") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("treatment", "control"))

opp_null
```

###

Our first three shuffles give 0.040, 0.120, and -0.013, the same three differences the chapter reports, because we used its seed; yours may differ. "Just one simulation will not be enough to get a sense of what sorts of differences would happen from chance alone."


###

````{verbatim}
opp_obs <- opportunity_cost |>
  specify(decision ~ group, success = "not buy video") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("treatment", "control"))

set.seed(25)
opp_null <- opportunity_cost |>
  specify(decision ~ group, success = "not buy video") |>
  hypothesize(null = "independence") |>
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") |>
  calculate(stat = "diff in props", order = c("treatment", "control"))
````

###

"The primary goal in this data analysis is to understand what sort of differences we might see if the null hypothesis were true, i.e., the treatment had no effect on students." `opp_null` is that understanding, written as 1,000 numbers.

```{r}
  summarize(mean_stat = mean(stat),
            n_extreme = sum(stat >= opp_obs$stat),
            prop_extreme = mean(stat >= opp_obs$stat))
```

###

The differences average 0.005, close to the zero we expect when the reminder does nothing, and only 6 of 1,000 reach the observed difference. Compare against the stored `opp_obs`, not a typed `0.2`: the computer stores 34/75 minus 19/75 as 0.19999999999999996, so a typed `0.2` misses the two shuffles that match it exactly.

"The **p-value** is the probability of observing data at least as favorable to the alternative hypothesis as our current dataset, if the null hypothesis were true." Ours is 0.006, the chapter's 6 in 1,000, and the 0.024 you found for the sex discrimination study was a p-value too.

### Exercise 11

Replace the code in that chunk with a small table that has one row for each study, sex discrimination and opportunity cost, showing its p-value and whether that p-value is below each of the thresholds 0.01, 0.05, and 0.10. Render.

```{r}
bind_rows(
  `Sex discrimination` = get_p_value(sex_null, obs_stat = sex_obs, direction = "greater"),
  `Opportunity cost` = get_p_value(opp_null, obs_stat = opp_obs, direction = "greater"),

  mutate(below_0.01 = p_value < 0.01,
         below_0.05 = p_value < 0.05,
         below_0.10 = p_value < 0.10)
```

###

"We say that the data provide **statistically discernible** evidence against the null hypothesis if the p-value is less than some predetermined threshold (e.g., 0.01, 0.05, 0.1)." The sex discrimination result is discernible at a **discernibility level** of 0.05 but not at 0.01, so the level must be chosen before looking at the data; the authors explain the usual choice in "[Why 0.05?](https://www.openintro.org/book/stat/why05/)"

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Chapter 11: Hypothesis testing with randomization](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/foundations-randomization.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You have learned to frame a research question as a null and an alternative hypothesis, to build a null distribution by shuffling the results of an experiment, and to measure the evidence against the null hypothesis with a p-value, using experiments on sex discrimination in promotions and on how students spend money.

The chapter's own summary, in the authors' words:

> [The chapter's closing figure] provides a visual summary of the randomization testing procedure.
>
> We can summarize the randomization test procedure as follows:
>
> -   **Frame the research question in terms of hypotheses.** Hypothesis tests are appropriate for research questions that can be summarized in two competing hypotheses. The null hypothesis $(H_0)$ usually represents a skeptical perspective or a perspective of no relationship between the variables. The alternative hypothesis $(H_A)$ usually represents a new view or the existence of a relationship between the variables.
> -   **Collect data with an observational study or experiment.** If a research question can be formed into two hypotheses, we can collect data to run a hypothesis test. If the research question focuses on associations between variables but does not concern causation, we would use an observational study. If the research question seeks a causal connection between two or more variables, then an experiment should be used.
> -   **Model the randomness that would occur if the null hypothesis was true.** In the examples above, the variability has been modeled as if the treatment (e.g., sexual identity, opportunity) allocation was independent of the outcome of the study. The computer generated null distribution is the result of many different randomizations and quantifies the variability that would be expected if the null hypothesis was true.
> -   **Analyze the data.** Choose an analysis technique appropriate for the data and identify the p-value. So far, we have only seen one analysis technique: randomization. Throughout the rest of this textbook, we'll encounter several new methods suitable for many other contexts.
> -   **Form a conclusion.** Using the p-value from the analysis, determine whether the data provide evidence against the null hypothesis. Also, be sure to write the conclusion in plain language so casual readers can understand the results.

For the two experiments, read Rosen and Jerdee's "[Influence of Sex Role Stereotypes on Personnel Decisions](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0035834)" and Frederick and colleagues' "[Opportunity Cost Neglect](https://doi.org/10.1086/599764)," the sources both help pages cite. For the choice of threshold, watch the authors' short video "[Why 0.05?](https://www.openintro.org/book/stat/why05/)"
